stories.issue: Can the US and China cooperate on AI and critical minerals without reducing their broader strategic rivalry?
stories.title: US–China talks put AI guardrails and critical minerals at the centre of strategic competition
stories.whatIsHappening: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are preparing for a Washington summit after senior US and Chinese officials discussed trade, AI and critical minerals. The US has proposed an incident-notification mechanism for serious AI risks, while China’s control over important minerals remains a major economic and security concern.
stories.argument: Limited cooperation on AI incidents, trade and minerals could create guardrails around the most dangerous points of interdependence while keeping commerce and supply chains functioning.
stories.otherSide: Technical cooperation can become another channel for strategic advantage or sensitive information. Without trust and enforceable commitments, a hotline or narrow deal may manage crises without changing the underlying competition over technology, supply chains and national power.
stories.whyItMatters: This relationship shapes the availability of chips, batteries, defence inputs, AI infrastructure and global investment. For India, the US–China balance affects its room to practise strategic autonomy and its opportunity to attract supply chains without becoming dependent on one bloc.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Separate crisis management from genuine strategic convergence. A communication channel can reduce accidental escalation, but it does not resolve export controls, critical-mineral dependence or the question of who sets technology standards. The practical test is whether cooperation produces verifiable risk reduction while preserving enough competition to protect national interests.
keyFacts: The Trump–Xi summit is scheduled in Washington this week, with AI, trade and critical minerals among the central issues.
US officials have proposed an AI incident-alert mechanism for serious safety or national-security events.
China remains a dominant supplier of critical minerals used in products including electric vehicles and defence systems.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Should countries cooperate on AI safety even when doing so may strengthen a strategic rival?

stories.issue: Can diplomacy make India’s energy outlook safer, or is the country still structurally exposed to external oil shocks?
stories.title: Oil falls on US–Iran diplomacy hopes, but India’s energy relief may be temporary
stories.whatIsHappening: Brent crude has eased toward $101 a barrel as markets watch possible US–Iran talks at the United Nations and a partial recovery in Saudi shipments. Reuters describes the move as relief for India rather than a reversal, because crude remains above $100 and the geopolitical risk is unresolved.
stories.argument: Diplomatic progress and restored shipments could lower India’s import bill, reduce imported inflation and give the rupee and current account some breathing room without requiring immediate, costly policy intervention.
stories.otherSide: Price relief driven by expectations can disappear quickly if talks fail or infrastructure and shipping risks return. Treating a temporary fall in crude as structural energy security could delay investment in diversification, storage and domestic alternatives.
stories.whyItMatters: Oil prices transmit geopolitics into Indian inflation, the rupee, fiscal choices, transport costs, corporate margins and household budgets. The issue is whether India should treat energy security mainly as a diplomatic problem, a market problem or a long-term transition problem.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Ask how durable the supply improvement is and who bears the risk if it reverses. Diplomacy can lower the immediate risk premium, but it cannot remove import dependence. A sensible strategy combines diversified suppliers and reserves with demand management and a transition that does not undermine affordability or reliability.
keyFacts: Brent crude hovered around $101 a barrel on September 22 after four consecutive sessions of decline.
Reuters reported that softer crude was easing pressure on India’s import bill, rupee, imported inflation and current account.
The same report said the relief remained incomplete because Brent was still above $100 and US–Iran tensions continued.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Should India spend more to insure against energy shocks even if that raises near-term costs?

stories.issue: Is India’s growth opportunity large enough to overcome concerns about tax certainty and regulatory predictability?
stories.title: India’s investment story is strong—but policy certainty remains part of the price
stories.whatIsHappening: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said investors remain positive about India’s long-term prospects but worry about inconsistent tax application and regulatory uncertainty. The report also notes near-8% growth in the latest quarter and nearly $100 billion in foreign direct investment in the financial year ended March.
stories.argument: Large domestic demand, strong growth and rising investment can make India attractive even when the business environment is imperfect; scale and opportunity can compensate for some friction.
stories.otherSide: Capital is mobile and long-term projects depend on predictable rules. Inconsistent taxes, regulation or enforcement can raise the risk premium, favour incumbents over new entrants and reduce the productivity benefits that foreign investment is supposed to create.
stories.whyItMatters: India wants foreign and domestic capital to fund manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and jobs. The debate is about whether headline growth is enough, or whether institutional predictability is a precondition for converting investor interest into broad-based productivity.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Distinguish the amount of capital from its quality and additionality. A large inflow can coexist with weak job creation if it is concentrated in protected or capital-intensive sectors. The stronger test is whether stable rules lower the cost of entry, support competition and help investment spread beyond a few large firms and cities.
keyFacts: The report says India attracted nearly $100 billion in FDI in the financial year ended March.
India’s latest quarterly growth was described as close to 8%.
The concern raised by investors was not the absence of opportunity, but inconsistent application of tax rules and policy uncertainty.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: What matters more for India’s next decade of investment: faster growth, lower taxes or more predictable rules?

stories.issue: Should India pursue full semiconductor fabrication, or first build strength in design, packaging, equipment and skills?
stories.title: India’s chip push is attracting capital—but the ecosystem must become commercially viable
stories.whatIsHappening: India has attracted investment pledges of as much as $12 billion from global and domestic players in the months after launching a new semiconductor policy. The commitments span equipment, materials, testing and assembly, with Tata and Micron among the companies involved in building a wider ecosystem.
stories.argument: A coordinated policy can overcome the high fixed costs and long learning periods of semiconductors, create strategic supply-chain capacity and connect India’s strengths in engineering and software with advanced manufacturing.
stories.otherSide: Capital commitments do not guarantee commercially competitive fabs. India may get better returns by building design, advanced packaging, equipment, materials and skilled talent first rather than trying to replicate the entire leading-edge manufacturing stack immediately.
stories.whyItMatters: Semiconductors sit at the intersection of national security, AI infrastructure, electronics manufacturing and industrial policy. The decision will determine whether India becomes a durable node in global technology supply chains or accumulates subsidised capacity without enough customers and know-how.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Evaluate the policy by ecosystem depth, not by announced dollars alone. Fabs need reliable power, water, suppliers, talent, customers and process know-how; packaging and design can create capabilities at lower capital intensity. The strategic case is strongest where public support unlocks learning and private demand, rather than replacing commercial discipline.
keyFacts: The report says investors have pledged as much as $12 billion toward India’s semiconductor push.
India announced a fresh semiconductor fund of $13.4 billion in July, according to the report.
The commitments include chip equipment, materials, chemicals, testing and assembly—not only wafer fabrication.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: Should India optimise for semiconductor sovereignty or for the fastest commercially viable role in the global chip supply chain?

stories.issue: Does renewed enthusiasm for AI prove that massive infrastructure spending is justified, or is the market still ahead of real productivity?
stories.title: The AI rally returns: adoption evidence or another test of investor conviction?
stories.whatIsHappening: Technology shares rebounded as investor enthusiasm returned after Meta’s Muse AI assistant gained attention. Reuters reported that Meta shares rose more than 11%, AMD reached a $1 trillion valuation, and semiconductor stocks advanced even as oil and bond yields created broader macroeconomic pressure.
stories.argument: Rapid adoption of useful AI tools can validate the enormous infrastructure investment by creating demand for chips, data centres and enterprise applications, while improving productivity over time.
stories.otherSide: Market enthusiasm and share-price gains do not prove that companies are earning durable returns on AI capital expenditure. High energy costs, uncertain monetisation and uneven productivity gains could leave investors and firms carrying the cost before the benefits arrive.
stories.whyItMatters: AI investment is becoming an economy-wide allocation decision, not just a technology trend. It affects capital markets, energy demand, semiconductor capacity, enterprise strategy and the future of Indian IT and services exports.
stories.howToThinkAboutIt: Separate three questions: whether users value the tools, whether firms can capture that value, and whether the infrastructure earns an adequate return. A strong view should distinguish adoption from profitable adoption and near-term market momentum from long-term changes in work and productivity.
keyFacts: Meta shares rose more than 11% on Monday after enthusiasm around its Muse AI assistant.
AMD reached a $1 trillion market value, while Intel and Arm rose 12.2% and 17%, respectively, in the Reuters report.
The rally occurred alongside renewed pressure from oil above $100 and higher bond yields, showing that AI investment remains connected to macroeconomic conditions.
stories.questionToThinkAbout: What evidence would convince you that the AI boom is creating durable productivity rather than mainly asset-price optimism?

extempore.issue: Should India pursue semiconductor sovereignty, or focus first on the parts of the global chip supply chain where it can become commercially competitive?
extempore.whyNow: India has attracted large semiconductor investment commitments while the US–China contest is making chips and critical minerals strategic assets. The immediate policy question is whether ambition should be measured by owning fabs or by building a profitable, resilient ecosystem around design, packaging, equipment and manufacturing.
argumentsFor: Domestic chip capacity can reduce strategic dependence and make India more credible in electronics, AI infrastructure and defence supply chains.
Large public support may be justified because semiconductor learning curves, infrastructure and supplier networks take years to develop.
India can connect its existing strengths in software, engineering and design with manufacturing, testing and packaging capabilities.
argumentsAgainst: Leading-edge fabs are extremely capital intensive and require specialised customers, utilities, suppliers and process expertise that subsidies cannot create instantly.
A focus on sovereignty can produce expensive capacity that is not globally competitive or commercially used.
India may build capability faster by specialising in design, advanced packaging, equipment, materials and mature-node production before moving up the stack.
examples: India’s reported $12 billion in semiconductor investment pledges across equipment, materials, testing and assembly.
The wider US–China contest over AI chips and critical minerals, which shows why supply-chain position has both commercial and strategic value.
facts: India announced a fresh $13.4 billion semiconductor fund in July, according to the Economic Times report.
Investment commitments span more than wafer fabrication, including equipment, materials, testing and assembly.
AI demand is increasing the strategic importance of chips while also raising the cost of infrastructure and capital.
